1:
Chrysostom frames the chapter as a second assault on ground already won. Nothing was ever more prepared for combat than the spirit of Paul — or rather, not his spirit, for he was not the inventor of these things, but the grace within him, which overcometh all things. What had been said before was enough to cast down the pride of the boasters about wisdom; but to enhance the splendour of the victory he contends anew for the points already affirmed, trampling upon the prostrate foe. He names the new move: Paul now shows that both the thing preached and the manner of preaching were enough to stagger people, and yet did not — not only are the disciples uneducated, but I myself also, who am the preacher.

On excellency of speech Robertson gives the lexicography: the noun means preeminence, rising above, and here excess or superfluity — not in excellence of rhetorical display or of philosophical subtlety. Henry works out what that excludes: Paul did not affect to appear a fine orator or deep philosopher, nor insinuate himself into their minds by a flourish of words or a pompous show of reason. Clarke names the local target — not with the arts of rhetoric used by your own philosophers — and adds why it was unnecessary: the testimony concerning Christ is so supremely excellent as to dignify any language by which it may be conveyed. Wesley: I did not affect either deep wisdom or eloquence.

What Paul declared is itself uncertain. Robertson reports the division: some manuscripts read the mystery of God, as at verse 7, others the testimony of God, as in the first chapter; he judges mystery correct, since Christ crucified is the mystery of God. He adds that Paul appropriated a word common among the mystery religions but puts into it his own ideas, the papyri giving many illustrations of it for doctrines known only to the initiated. Ellicott, reading testimony, takes it as Paul’s witness concerning God in Christ. Calvin observes what the concession is for: Paul allows he had none of the aids of human eloquence or wisdom, but in acknowledging himself destitute of them he hints at the inference — that the power of God shone the more illustriously in his ministry, from standing in no need of such helps.

The second verse turns on where the negative goes. Ellicott renders it, I did not determine to know: the only subject concerning which the apostle had formed a determined resolve was the preaching of Christ, and of him as crucified. Robertson agrees on the construction, the negative going with the verb and not the pronoun. Barnes gets there through the word know, taken in the sense of attend to or regard: I resolved not to give my time while among you to the laws and traditions of the Jews, to your orators, philosophers and poets, to your architecture or statuary, but to attend to this only.

Both moderns insist the resolution cost something. Barnes points out that Paul formed it knowing the Greeks’ peculiar fondness for subtle disquisitions and finished elocution, and fully aware that the theme would excite derision and contempt. Ellicott presses the historical distance: we can scarcely realise the stumbling-block which the preaching of a crucified Christ must have been, for to us it is illumined with the glories of eighteen centuries, whereas to every Jew and Gentile it conveyed but one idea, that of the most revolting and degrading punishment. Robertson adds the biography: he stuck to it even after Athens, where he was practically laughed out of court. Henry states the positive side — Christ, in his person and offices, is the sum and substance of the gospel, and anyone who heard Paul preach found him harp continually on this string — and Gill notes what was given up, Paul being well versed in human literature.
3:
What the weakness was comes first. Gill offers three answers: the weakness of his bodily presence and the contemptibleness of his voice; or his lowly deportment, working with his own hands rather than exerting authority; or the persecutions he endured for preaching a crucified Christ. Clarke thinks there was something in his speech unfavourable to ready elocution and some bodily infirmity besides, and illustrates by contrast: Louis the Fourteenth styled Peter du Bosc the finest speaker in his kingdom, yet look at his works and it is difficult to subscribe to the saying — solved by the information that his person was princely and his voice majestic. Paul had none of these advantages, and yet idolatry and superstition fell before him: thus God was seen in the work, and the man was forgotten. Wesley divides the three: weakness of body, fear lest he offend any, and much trembling — the emotion of my mind affecting my very body.

Ellicott will not reduce the fear to modesty. There was in it, he grants, much of the self-distrust which so sensitive a nature would feel in so exalted a mission; but he cannot think the allusion is only to that, since there is also a physical apprehension of danger — the bravest being not those who feel no fear, but those who keenly appreciate danger and yet by their moral might conquer the dread. He finds three traces: Be not afraid, spoken at Corinth; Be of good cheer, Paul, after the scene before Ananias; Fear not, Paul, in the shipwreck. Robertson supplies the itinerary — prison at Philippi, driven out of Thessalonica and Beroea, politely bowed out of Athens — and calls it a human touch to see this shrinking, adding that cool complacency is not the mood of the finest preaching.

The phrase for enticing words is the sharpest philological problem here. Robertson concedes it looks like a false disclaimer, since surely a preacher desires to be persuasive, then notes the adjective has not been found anywhere else and seems formed directly from the verb to persuade; the kindred noun is used elsewhere of the plausible Gnostic philosophers, and gullible people are easy marks for such plausible pulpiteers. Calvin reports the same rarity as a textual problem: the word occurs nowhere else in the New Testament or in classical authors, so some suppose a corruption of the reading. Clarke has two variants: two ancient manuscripts read revelation for demonstration, and most of the best manuscripts and fathers leave out the adjective before wisdom.

What the demonstration consisted of divides them. Barnes makes it specific: the miracles, the gift of tongues, and the remarkable conversions that attended the preaching. Calvin refuses the narrowing: most restrict it to miracles, but he takes it more generally, as the hand of God powerfully exercised. Ellicott draws the consequence: the demonstration was the result of no human art or skill, and therefore the Corinthians could glory in no human teacher. Cyril of Jerusalem does not expound the verse but cites it, to prove Paul was full of the Holy Ghost.

The last verse states the purpose, and Calvin argues it from the contrary. Had the apostle’s preaching rested on the power of eloquence, it might have been overthrown by superior eloquence; that must have been most powerful which could stand of itself without foreign aid, and it is the property of faith to rest upon God alone. Gill puts it negatively: faith must not stand on so sandy a foundation as one that might be puffed away by a superior flow and force of words. Barnes turns it inward: every Christian has in his own experience furnished demonstration that the religion he loves is from God. Robertson points outward: one has only to instance the changing theories of men about science, philosophy, religion and politics to see that faith’s only secure rest is God’s power.
6:
Chrysostom answers the charge of foolishness with a parable of sailing. Darkness suits those diseased in their eyesight better than light, and it is the same with spiritual wisdom: as the wisdom of God seemed foolishness to those without, so their own wisdom, being foolishness indeed, was accounted by them wisdom. The result has been as if a man skilled in navigation promised to cross a boundless tract of sea without ship or sails, while another, ignorant of it all, committing himself to a ship and a steersman and sailors, sailed over in safety — the seeming ignorance of this man being wiser than the wisdom of the other. Excellent is the art of managing a ship, but when it makes too great professions it is a kind of folly — as is every art not contented with its own proper limits. He notes the order too: after our proofs, not before, are we best able to abash the gainsayers.

Who the perfect are divides them four ways. Barnes takes it of those advanced in Christian knowledge, denying it means sinless; and he suspects an allusion to the heathen mysteries, where the fully initiated were said to be perfect. Robertson refuses that outright: Paul is not distinguishing exoteric from esoteric wisdom, but marking the necessary difference in teaching for babes and grown men — some at Corinth being old babes, unable in spite of their years to digest solid spiritual food. Ellicott agrees they are the grown up, then claims what the others do not: this wisdom the apostle had not in fact taught the Corinthians, having given them only the alphabet of Christianity because they were still babes. Calvin declines all this. By the perfect he means not those who had attained a wisdom full and complete, but those of sound and unbiased judgment; and he turns it against the objectors, since if the doctrine is disrelished by any, they give sufficient evidence by that token that they possess a depraved and vitiated understanding.

Wesley narrows the wisdom rather than the hearers: by wisdom the apostle seems to mean not the whole Christian doctrine, but the most sublime and abstruse parts of it, spoken among adult and experienced Christians. Clarke, reporting a Hebraist, distinguishes four wisdoms — the heathen wisdom of the Gentile philosophers, which the Jews called Grecian wisdom and undervalued so far as to join two curses in a breath, cursed is he that breeds hogs and cursed is he who teaches his son Grecian wisdom; the Jewish wisdom of the scribes and Pharisees who crucified the Lord; the Gospel, which is the wisdom of God in a mystery; and the wisdom of this world, the system the Jews made up out of their own doctors.

Ellicott points out that the sentence is sharper in Greek, since at the fourth verse the word is simply wisdom and not man’s wisdom, so this assertion verbally contradicts that one. On the closing participle he prefers which are being brought to nought, the reference being not to the transitoriness of human wisdom but to God’s bringing them to nothing by rejecting them. Robertson reads it as gradual: the nullification of these rulers goes on before the final triumph of Christ in his kingdom. Wesley sweeps all into the clause: both they and their wisdom, and the world itself.

Henry states the principle: those who are wise themselves are the only proper judges of what is wisdom, and those who receive the doctrine as divine discern in it the deep and admirable designs of the divine wisdom. How different, he adds, is the judgment of God from the world’s — he seeth not as man seeth. Gill states it defensively: the apostle vindicates his preaching from the charge of folly, for it was not folly but wisdom he and his fellow ministers preached, and that of the highest kind.
7:
What mystery means divides them at once. Barnes insists it is not obscurity: even and wisdom were supplied by the translators. He does not say their preaching was mysterious, but that this wisdom had been hidden from men until then; for the word with us commonly means what is beyond comprehension, which is not its usual sense in Scripture, where it denotes what is concealed. Ellicott takes the opposite line, that the apostle is describing his method: he dealt with the wisdom as the ancient mysteries were dealt with, explaining certain truths only to the initiated. Robertson will not settle which word the phrase attaches to, wisdom or we speak, the result differing little; he prefers wisdom, so long a secret and now at last revealed. Clarke dates the concealment from the settling of the Jewish economy, and observes that though the gospel was announced by the prophets and prefigured by the law, the most intelligent of the Jewish rulers had no adequate knowledge of it.

Calvin explains why such wisdom goes unesteemed. The gospel so far transcends the perspicacity of human intellect that to whatever height men of superior intellect raise their view they can never reach it, while meanwhile they despise its meanness, as if it lay prostrate at their feet; and the more proudly they contemn it, the farther they are from acquaintance with it. He then guards it pastorally: since Paul has called the gospel a hidden thing, there was danger that believers should be appalled and retire in despair, and so he adds that it has nevertheless been appointed to us, that we might enjoy it.

On the ordaining before the world Robertson notes an aorist of God’s elective purpose as shown in Christ crucified — it was no afterthought or change of plan — and reads unto our glory as the glory of inward enlightenment as well as outward exaltation.

Who the princes were is the most canvassed question here. Gill runs through three candidates: not the devils, who had they known what God designed by Christ’s death would never have been concerned in bringing it about; nor so much the political governors, Herod and Pilate, who were also entirely ignorant; but the ecclesiastical rulers of the Jewish church state, the priests, scribes, Pharisees and learned doctors. Clarke agrees that this world here means the Jewish state and its rulers. Barnes takes in both parties, and refuses them the excuse: their ignorance arose from not understanding the prophecies and from an unwillingness to be convinced, so that if they had not full knowledge it was their own fault. Calvin declines the sorting and reads the negative as a general statement, since Scripture speaks in terms of universality of what happens for the most part, so a few men of distinction may well have had the pure knowledge of God. He names both parties — the chief men of the Jews, high in credit for holiness and wisdom, and Pilate and the Roman empire — as a most distinct proof of the utter blindness of those wise only according to the flesh.

The title draws the sharpest comment. Robertson takes it as a genitive of characterisation, bringing out the contrast between the indignity of the Cross and the majesty of the Victim, and recalls that Peter at Pentecost dwelt on the ignorance of the Jews in crucifying Christ as their only hope of repentance. Ellicott says it stands in striking contrast to the ignominy of the crucifixion, and that the conduct of the princes and rulers, alike Jewish and Gentile, proves the previous assertion. Wesley alone turns it into a doctrine: the giving of this august title, peculiar to the great Jehovah, plainly shows Christ to be the supreme God; and since the Father is styled the Father of glory and the Holy Ghost the Spirit of glory, the title belongs to all three.
9:
Where the quotation comes from is the hardest question here, and nobody settles it. Ellicott states it plainly: the words are not to be found as here given anywhere in the Old Testament. He reports the guesses — an apocryphal or lost book, or a reference not to a writing but to historical facts — and rejects them, since none would justify the formula it is written, confined in the apostolic writings to the Old Testament. His own answer is memory: phrases scattered through Isaiah would easily be joined and resemble even verbally the passage written here. Robertson agrees, taking it for a free chain of quotations from three passages of Isaiah. Calvin is the most troubled: two very great difficulties present themselves, that the words quoted do not correspond with the prophet’s, and that Paul seems to have turned the prophet’s declaration to a purpose foreign to his design.

They agree, against the popular use of the verse, that it is not about heaven. Barnes calls the objections insuperable: the Isaiah passage has no such reference, and the apostle’s object here is not to describe the future state but to prove that Christians have true wisdom. Clarke concurs, the words belonging certainly to the present state and expressing the wondrous light, life and liberty which the Gospel communicates, adding that such a scheme, in which God’s glory and man’s felicity should be equally secured, could have been conceived by no mind but God’s. Gill grants the future glories are indeed inconceivable, but says the context shows the doctrines of grace are meant. Robertson puts it shortest: the dominant idea is the present blessing to those who love God, and we need not wait for heaven to see them.

On the revelation the emphasis falls on the pronoun. Ellicott makes us the emphatic word — none of the princes of this age know these things, but God hath revealed them unto us his apostles and teachers . Barnes widens it in three stages: first to the apostles, then to the church through their inspired instructors, then to all Christians by the illuminating agency of the Spirit. Robertson dates it at the entry of the Gospel into the world rather than, as one commentator has it, at admission to the Church.

The verb searcheth is glossed carefully. Ellicott insists it does not convey inquiry for the purpose of acquiring knowledge, but complete and accurate knowledge itself. Calvin defines the object: by the deep things understand not secret judgments, which we are forbidden to pry into, but the entire doctrine of salvation. Wesley names what is revealed: peace and joy unspeakable, by the Spirit who fully knows them. Calvin draws a consolation: the blunter the human intellect for the mysteries of God, the surer our faith, resting on the revelation of the Spirit — and in this we recognise the unbounded goodness of God, who makes our defect contribute to our advantage.

Two turn the verse into doctrine, from opposite ends of the tradition. Henry finds here a proof of the divine authority of the Scriptures, and then of the divinity of the Holy Ghost: no one can know the things of God but his Holy Spirit, who is one with the Father and the Son — most clear testimony, he says, to the real Godhead and the distinct person of the Spirit. Cyril of Jerusalem gets there first: believe thou also in the Holy Ghost, and hold the same opinion concerning him which thou hast received to hold concerning the Father and the Son; learn that this Holy Spirit is one, indivisible, of manifold power, not himself divided, who searcheth all things, even the deep things of God. At the preceding verse he had used the same text the other way: if the things God hath prepared are incomprehensible to our thoughts, how can we comprehend him who hath prepared them?
11:
The argument is an analogy, and those who handle it carefully mark where it stops. Barnes states it: no man can know his own mind and intentions but himself, and unless he chooses to reveal them others cannot ascertain them — so of God, whose designs no man can penetrate. But it is not to be supposed, he adds, that there is a perfect resemblance between the soul’s relation to the man and the Spirit’s relation to God. Robertson makes the same guard grammatically, noting the absence in the second clause of the phrase that is in him: it is not the mere self-consciousness of God but the personal Holy Spirit in his relation to God the Father.

Clarke turns aside to the text. The word for man in the first clause is omitted by the Alexandrian manuscript and one other, and by several fathers, and one bishop contends against its authenticity, reading instead, what is there that knoweth the things of a man, except the spirit of a man that is in him? To say what man, except the spirit of a man, is to speak improperly, and to suppose that the spirit of a man is a man. Clarke grants the authority is slender but says the omission renders the text much more intelligible. Ellicott renders in the same direction — who of men knoweth the things of a man? — and then guards the second clause: the words are not an assertion that man can have no knowledge of the things of God, but that man as man cannot know them, his knowledge being in virtue of the Spirit of God dwelling in him.

Wesley draws the inference the others leave implicit: the things of God knoweth no one but the Spirit, who, consequently, is God.

What the spirit of the world is divides them. Gill offers three: Satan, the god of the world; or the carnal disposition of the men of the world, a spirit of covetousness, pride, malice and error; or rather the carnal wisdom of the world. Clarke narrows it historically, as he narrowed the princes: it is the spirit of the Jewish teachers, looking for a worldly kingdom and a worldly Messiah, and interpreting the Old Testament in a carnal sense. Robertson keeps it inside the chapter, taking it for the wisdom of this age already named at the sixth verse. Wesley makes a distinction the rest do not: this spirit is not properly received at all, for the men of the world always had it, whereas Christians receive the Spirit of God, which before they had not.

Who the we are is disputed in the same breath. Barnes takes it of Christians, and especially the apostles, since the following verse shows he had himself and his colleagues chiefly in view. Ellicott insists it must not be confined to the apostles: though referring primarily to them it includes all the members of the Christian Church. Calvin turns the verse into a weapon. The Spirit of revelation which we have received is not of the world, so as to be merely creeping upon the ground, subject to vanity, fluctuating, holding us in doubt and perplexity; on the contrary it is from God, and hence above all heavens, of solid and unvarying truth, placed above all risk of doubt. The passage is most abundantly clear, he says, for refuting the doctrine of a constant hesitancy on the part of believers, which allows no assurance of salvation but what hangs on probable conjecture. Robertson finds the same in the purpose clause: it is not a senseless rhapsody or secret mystery, but God expects us to understand what he has freely given. Cyril of Jerusalem, meanwhile, is collecting the Spirit’s names — the Spirit of holiness, of adoption, of revelation, of promise, of grace, and in the Psalms the good Spirit and the princely Spirit.
13:
Robertson reads the three verses as a sequence and names it: there is revelation at the tenth verse, illumination at the twelfth, and inspiration here, so that Paul claims the help of the Holy Spirit for the reception of the revelation, for the understanding of it, and for the expression of it. He notes that the verb for speak is one which in the papyri calls attention to the form of utterance rather than the substance.

The closing clause is the crux, and the two who work at it reach different answers. Clarke rejects the common reading, that spiritual things under the Old Testament are compared with spiritual things under the New: the verb rather signifies conferring or explaining, and the second word should be rendered to spiritual men, so that the sense is, explaining spiritual things to spiritual persons. Ellicott prefers, explaining spiritual things in spiritual language, supporting it from the Septuagint, where the word is used of expounding, especially of dreams, the dream being as it were compared with its interpretation; the other rendering, he grants, involves a use of the word not found elsewhere in the New Testament. Wesley offers both and chooses neither: explaining spiritual things by spiritual words, or adapting spiritual words to spiritual things.

On the style that is refused, Clarke sets two schools side by side. The Greek orators affected a high and florid language, full of tropes and figures, which dazzled more than it enlightened; the rabbins affected obscurity, studious to find cabalistical meanings which had no tendency to make the people wise unto salvation; the apostles could follow neither, but spoke the things of God in the words of God. Calvin describes the same refusal from the other end: the words rejected savour of human learning, polished by the rules of the rhetoricians or blown up with philosophical loftiness to excite the admiration of the hearers, whereas spiritual words are adapted to a pure and simple style, answering to the dignity of the Spirit rather than to empty ostentation. Barnes draws the doctrinal consequence: the passage is full proof that the apostles laid claim to divine inspiration.

The natural man then divides them sharply, and the division is about psychology. Ellicott builds a trichotomy: our ordinary way of speaking of man as soul and body is altogether inaccurate, for true psychology regards man as a trinity of natures — body, soul and spirit — the first our physical nature, the second our intellectual nature, embracing desires and human affections, the third our spiritual nature. Barnes and Clarke take the word downward: it denotes those governed by the natural instincts and animal passions, so that sensual would correctly express the idea, the Greeks using it of what man has in common with the brutes. Calvin refuses that outright: by the natural man he does not mean, as is commonly thought, the man given up to gross lusts or to his own sensuality, but any man endowed with nothing more than the faculties of nature. Gill agrees and makes it concrete: not a babe in Christ, nor the openly profane, but the wise philosopher, the scribe, the disputer of this world, the man of the highest attainments in nature, in whom reason is wrought up to its highest pitch.

Wesley states the incapacity in three clauses: receiveth not, that is, does not understand or conceive; neither can he know them, for as he has not the will, so neither has he the power; and they are spiritually discerned, being discernible only by the aid of that Spirit, and by those spiritual senses, which he has not. Cyril of Jerusalem takes the verse as a rule for his own lecturing: he will not use the subtleties of men, for that is unprofitable, but merely call to mind what comes from the divine Scriptures — the safest course, according to the blessed Apostle Paul.
15:
How far the judging extends is settled first. Barnes limits it: not absolutely all things, nor that the spiritual man is omniscient, but that he sees those things the apostle has in view, what is revealed by the Spirit. He turns the second clause into observation rather than doctrine: the spiritual man’s feelings, principles, hopes, fears and joys cannot be fully understood by any natural man, who does not comprehend the principles that actuate him, does not enter into his joys, does not sympathise with him.

Gill spends his note refusing a candidate. The verse means no particular individual, and not the pope of Rome, as his adherents vainly imagine, whom they fancy a supreme and infallible judge in things spiritual, from whose judgment there is no appeal and who himself comes under the judgment of none — for he is so far from being a spiritual man that he stands described as the man of sin, the son of perdition. Nor does it mean others who might claim it: not those only outwardly reformed, who are at best moral and not spiritual men; nor all who have spiritual gifts, which may be where there is no spiritual grace.

Clarke reports a second rendering and declines it. Some suppose the verb should be understood as examines, convinces, reproves, and read the verse accordingly: the spiritual man, the well-taught Christian, can easily convict every animal man of error and vice, yet is himself convicted of no man, his mind being enlightened and his life holy. This is a good sense, says Clarke, but the first seems the most natural. Robertson keeps the plain sense: the spiritual man is qualified to sift, to examine, to decide rightly, because the eyes of his heart are enlightened, whereas men of intellectual gifts ignorant of the things of Christ talk learnedly and patronisingly about things of which they are grossly ignorant. Men will pass judgment on him, but he refuses to accept the decision of his ignorant judges — as Polycarp did, preferring to be burnt rather than say Lord Caesar in place of Lord Jesus.

Calvin moves the prerogative off the man. It is not ascribed to the man as an individual, but to the word of God, which the spiritual follow in judging; and the assurance of faith is not subject to men, as though they could make it totter at their nod, being superior even to the angels themselves.

The closing quotation is a denial. Barnes says the interrogative form strongly denies that anyone has known the mind of the Lord: as no one can fully understand God by nature, neither can he understand the man who is influenced by God and is like him, so that it is not to be wondered at if he regards the Christian religion as folly and the Christian as a fool. Calvin traces it to Isaiah, where the prophet asks who hath been God’s counsellor, and says the interrogation teaches that the secret counsel contained in the gospel is far removed from the understanding of men. Clarke corrects the translation: the words rendered that he may instruct him should be, that he may teach it — the mind of God — not instruct God, but teach his mind to others, which the Hebrew will also bear. On the last clause Ellicott notes that the apostle identifies Christ with the Spirit, of whom he has been speaking as the teacher of spiritual things, and guards the claim: he does not mean the apostles knew all that the mind of Christ knew, but that all they did know was from him. Calvin leaves the reference open between believers universally and ministers exclusively, preferring the narrower; and Wesley settles it the same way — we, that is, spiritual men, apostles in particular, who know and understand the mind of Christ concerning the whole plan of gospel salvation.
